extracted.intended_audience: Educational institution officials (Title IX coordinators, administrators), legal counsel, and OCR reviewers/analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing how recipients (K–12 and postsecondary institutions) must respond to allegations of Title IX sexual harassment, including supportive measures, grievance-process obligations, OCR review standard, and emergency removals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer Supportive Measures (§106.44(a) and §106.45(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient's response must treat complainants and respondents equitably by offering supportive measures as defined in §106.30; a Title IX Coordinator must promptly contact the complainant to discuss availability of supportive measures, consider the complainant's wishes with respect to supportive measures, inform the complainant of the availability of supportive measures with or without the filing of a formal complaint, and explain the process for filing a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients are required to offer supportive measures to complainants whether or not a formal complaint is filed; this mandate places recipients on notice that they must offer supportive measures. The Title IX Coordinator's prompt contact, discussion, and explanation of filing options are explicit duties. (See also §106.45(b)(1) requiring compliance with §106.44(a) with or without a formal complaint.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive Measures Definition and Non-Punitive Nature (§106.30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures are expressly defined as non-disciplinary, non-punitive individualized services offered as appropriate, as reasonably available, and without fee or charge to the complainant or the respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures must not have punitive or disciplinary consequences for either complainants or respondents. They are intended to restore or preserve access to the recipient's education program or activity without imposing sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation When Not Providing Supportive Measures (§106.45(b)(10)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a recipient does not provide a complainant with supportive measures, the recipient must document why such a response was not clearly unreasonable in light of the known circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This documentation requirement ensures accountability when supportive measures are withheld and removes any safe-harbor effect for merely offering minimal measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive Measures Alone May Be Insufficient (No Safe Harbor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations do not include the proposed safe harbor that a recipient is not deliberately indifferent when, in the absence of a formal complaint, the recipient offers and implements supportive measures and informs the complainant in writing of the right to file a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering supportive measures does not automatically satisfy the deliberate indifference standard; depending on facts, a non-deliberately indifferent response may require initiating the formal grievance process (including the Title IX Coordinator signing a formal complaint). The safe harbor was removed because recipients are required to offer supportive measures and must document when they do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complainant's Right to File Later; Participation Condition on Filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to impose a statute of limitations on filing a formal complaint; instead, at the time of filing a formal complaint the complainant must be participating in or attempting to participate in the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'participation or attempting to participate' requirement is a reasonable condition on the ability to require investigation and is broadly interpreted (e.g., withdrawn students who wish to re-enroll, graduates who wish to attend alumni events, leaves of absence). Separately, §106.45(b)(3)(ii) gives recipients discretion to dismiss a formal complaint where the respondent is no longer enrolled or employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on Coercion or Retaliation (§106.71)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are expressly forbidden from threatening, intimidating, coercing, or discriminating against any complainant for the purpose of chilling the complainant's exercise of any rights under Title IX, including the right to file a formal complaint and to receive supportive measures even if the complainant chooses not to file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision protects complainant autonomy and responds to concerns that institutions might coerce complainants into accepting supportive measures in lieu of a formal grievance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCR Will Not Re-Weigh the Evidence Solely Because It Would Have Decided Differently (§106.44(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department will not overturn the outcome of a Title IX grievance process solely because the Department (or OCR) might have weighed the evidence differently from the recipient's decision-maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limited deference is intended to promote finality and avoid de novo factfinding by OCR on every determination, but it does not limit OCR's ability to evaluate compliance with Title IX or to set aside determinations when recipients fail to comply with regulatory requirements, commit gross/malicious violations, or otherwise affect outcome integrity. The provision applies neutrally to determinations that find respondents responsible or not responsible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of §106.44(b)(2) and OCR Review Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The deference described in §106.44(b)(2) applies only to determinations regarding responsibility reached through the §106.45 grievance process (which applies to formal complaints of sexual harassment); complaints about other types of sex discrimination are processed under the prompt and equitable grievance procedures required by §106.8.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing in §106.44(b)(2) precludes a person from filing a complaint with OCR, and OCR retains full authority to investigate, identify patterns or practices of discrimination, and enforce Title IX and its implementing regulations. The Department may give due weight to EEOC determinations where applicable, but these Title IX regulations do not govern EEOC procedures under Title VII.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance Process Procedural and Substantive Requirements (§106.45)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recipient investigates a formal complaint of sexual harassment, the grievance process must: treat complainants and respondents equitably by providing remedies for complainants when a respondent is found responsible and by following a grievance process prior to imposing disciplinary sanctions on respondents; objectively evaluate all relevant evidence and give both parties equal opportunity to present witnesses and evidence; avoid bias or conflicts of interest; and resolve allegations under designated, reasonably prompt time frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These prescribed procedures are designed to produce reliable outcomes; failure to comply with §106.45's requirements can lead OCR to hold recipients accountable and, where necessary, set aside determinations in order to remedy regulatory violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency Removal Standards and Related Safeguards (§106.44(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section §106.44(c) permits emergency removal of a respondent where there is an immediate threat to the physical health or safety of students or employees, allowing institutions latitude to address safety emergencies while balancing due process protections for respondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters urged (and the discussion addresses) several limiting safeguards or clarifications: require individualized threat/risk assessments; narrowly tailor removals to what is strictly necessary to mitigate health/safety risks; base removals on objective evidence and, where appropriate, licensed/qualified evaluators; define what constitutes an immediate threat (health vs. safety vs. physical); require periodic review of emergency removals to prevent indefinite suspension; provide alternative academic accommodations and access to classes/exams for removed respondents; mitigate harm to respondents later found not responsible (e.g., opportunity to retake missed work); secure and protect a removed person's personal property; and consider whether emergency removals should also address threats of illegal conduct or obstruction of evidence. These are implementation expectations and concerns reflected in the preamble that recipients should address when using emergency removal authority.
